vopros: Should I pay for a tool that tracks whether ChatGPT and other AI assistants mention my business, or hire someone to get my business recommended by AI?

vyzhimka.tekst:
This isn't strictly an either/or choice — the two options serve different purposes and often work best together. Here's how to think about it.

## What tracking tools actually do (and don't do)

Tools like Otterly, Profound, Writesonic GEO, Semrush AI Visibility Toolkit, and similar platforms work by automatically sending queries to AI search engines like ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, and AI Mode, and analyzing the responses for brand mentions, citations, and source links. They give you dashboards on brand coverage rate, share of voice compared to competitors, platform-by-platform visibility, and trends over time.

Pricing is fairly accessible — entry-level tools start around $29/month with a free trial, while more full-featured platforms like Writesonic GEO starts at $79/month when billed annually. Enterprise platforms with broader coverage across engines like Copilot, Grok, and Meta AI cost more.

**The catch:** most of these tools are measurement instruments, not fix-it tools. As one guide on tracking tools put it: "Tracking tells you where you're losing; fixing it is a separate job." A few newer platforms are trying to close that gap — for example, Writesonic's approach provides specific guidance on how to improve your content to increase AI visibility... the platform suggests content changes, structure, formatting, topic coverage, and source-worthiness signals — but even these are recommendations, not execution.

## What actually gets you recommended

This is the more important part, because it explains why a tracker alone won't move the needle. AI recommendation engines work very differently from paid search — there's no ad auction to buy your way in: you can't pay to show up in ChatGPT. Unlike Google Ads, no direct payment mechanism exists for AI recommendations. Authority must be earned through strategic presence-building.

What actually influences whether you get mentioned:

- **Third-party authority signals.** ChatGPT combines two layers: the knowledge inside the model itself and, for current or commercial questions, live web results. Both layers lean on external sources: editorial media, Wikipedia, review sites, forums and LinkedIn. If you appear in those sources, you stand a chance of a recommendation. If you don't, you're rarely mentioned spontaneously. A mapping of citation sources found Reddit, YouTube, LinkedIn, Wikipedia, Forbes, G2, Yelp, Facebook, Medium and TechRadar make up the top ten across all major AI platforms.

- **Reviews matter a lot for local/service businesses.** Review signals weigh heavily in AI recommendations — count, rating, recency, response rate, and what reviewers actually say, with benchmarks suggesting 150+ reviews per location as the level below which AI assistants rarely name a business, and a 4.2–4.7 star average.

- **Website clarity and evidence.** Strengthening revenue-critical service pages, correcting inconsistent business information, adding credible evidence, and ensuring search systems can access your site give ChatGPT a stronger reason to recognize, cite, and recommend your company.

- **This is genuinely unpaid, earned work.** The whole playbook is unpaid, unbuyable positioning. Getting a mention often comes down to things like local news coverage — emailing the business reporter at your local paper or TV station when you hit a milestone, since local journalists are under-pitched and often looking for story angles.

## So which should you pay for?

**A tracking tool alone** makes sense if:
- You just want a baseline / early warning system for how you're currently showing up
- You have in-house marketing capacity to act on what you learn
- Budget is tight — $29–79/month is low-risk

You can even get a rough baseline for free without a subscription: open ChatGPT, ask it who it recommends for your core service in your city, do the same with Google AI Overviews and Perplexity, and write down what comes back — if your business isn't named, you have a clear baseline.

**Hiring someone (a GEO/AI-search specialist or agency)** makes more sense if:
- You've confirmed you're invisible or misrepresented and don't have time/expertise to fix it yourself
- The fix involves sustained work — PR outreach, review generation systems, structured content rewrites, schema markup — that's genuinely a specialist skill set, not a one-time task

**The realistic combo most businesses land on:** use a cheap/free tracker to establish where you stand and monitor progress, then either DIY the fixes (reviews, PR pitches, content updates) using published playbooks, or hire a specialist specifically for the execution work rather than paying indefinitely for monitoring alone. Given every review, every news mention, every directory listing, every blog article that names your business in a relevant context is a data point that the AI accumulates into a confidence score, the highest-leverage spend is usually on generating those third-party signals — not on the dashboard that watches for them.

One caveat: this space is moving fast and many "reviews" of these tools are themselves marketing content from competing vendors, so treat specific tool recommendations (including from me) with some skepticism and try free trials before committing to annual contracts.
